edges.description: The authors propose that decreased dopamine reactivity contributes to the negative emotionality they measured, which they gloss as increased stress reactivity and irritability. The proposal is theirs and is conditional.
Weight loss is among the frequently reported features of the withdrawal syndrome.
Meeting the withdrawal criteria was associated with a shorter duration of abstinence.
Repeated failure to sustain abstinence is what the diagnosis describes.
Chronic daily smoking is the condition under which cortical CB1 receptors are found downregulated, and the magnitude tracks its duration.
The blunted dopamine response was measured in people who use cannabis against controls, so the exposure is what distinguishes the groups.

nodes.description: Challenged with methylphenidate, people who use cannabis show markedly blunted dopamine responses on positron emission tomography. The precise claim matters and is easy to overstate: baseline striatal D2 receptor availability did not differ from controls, so this is reduced reactivity to a dopamine challenge and not receptor downregulation. In the ventral striatum the response was inversely correlated with negative emotionality, which was higher in the cannabis group, and with addiction severity and craving. The authors read it as consistent with decreased brain reactivity that might contribute to negative emotionality and addictive behaviour, and the entry keeps that conditional.

nodes.description:
A withdrawal syndrome reliably follows discontinuation of chronic heavy cannabis use, with onset and time course resembling other substance withdrawal syndromes. Its symptoms are predominantly emotional and behavioural; appetite change, weight loss and physical discomfort are also frequently reported. In a sample of 384 adult lifetime cannabis smokers reporting retrospectively on their most difficult unaided quit attempt, 40.9 per cent met the DSM-5 threshold, and meeting it was associated with the duration and frequency of prior use.
The entry binds only the withdrawal features its sources name. Neither cited source enumerates the seven DSM-5 criterion symptoms in the text available here, so individually bound phenotypes stop at weight loss, which is stated. Appetite change is described without a direction in the source and is left as prose rather than bound to a decreased-appetite term, because the direction would be inferred rather than read.

nodes.description:
Chronic daily cannabis smokers show downregulated CB1 receptors on positron emission tomography. Two features of the finding constrain how it can be used: it is selective to cortical regions rather than striatal, so it is not a change in the reward pathway the acute nodes describe; and it reverses, with receptor density returning to normal after about four weeks of monitored abstinence. The magnitude tracks years of smoking. The authors describe it as a neuroadaptation that may promote dependence, and that hedge is kept.
One annotation is looser than the measurement behind it. The study measured receptor density by tracer binding, and the slot binds GO:0004949 cannabinoid receptor activity, which is a function term; the preferred_term says availability. Density and activity are not the same quantity, and the entry does not claim a measured change in signalling through the receptor. No GO or PATO term for receptor availability was found, so the function term stands in for it and this paragraph records the gap rather than leaving the binding to imply more than the data.

nodes.description:
Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol raises accumbens shell dopamine in rats. In humans the same effect is much weaker: a pooled re-analysis of two raclopride positron emission tomography studies found a small, statistically significant reduction in binding in limbic striatum, about three and a half per cent, and nothing elsewhere in the striatum, and its authors introduce their own work by noting that previous human imaging of this question had given inconsistent results. The node is therefore marked provisional, and is scoped to the animal result with the human magnitude recorded beside it rather than averaged into it. This is the point at which the entry departs most from its stimulant siblings, where the human dopamine signal is large and uncontested.
The subregional detail this node's prose rests on is not queryable from its binding. UBERON:0001882 nucleus accumbens is the most specific term available, and the shell, which is where the animal effect was localised and where it did not extend to the core, survives only in preferred_term. The same term is bound on the blunted-reactivity node for ventral striatum, so the two nodes are indistinguishable by anatomy in the graph even though the studies behind them measured different things.

nodes.description: The dopamine effect of delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol depends on mu1 opioid receptors in the ventral tegmentum, not on the cannabinoid receptor alone. Infusing a mu1 antagonist into the ventral tegmentum abolishes the effect of cannabinoids on accumbens dopamine, and does so for heroin as well, which is the sense in which the two drugs share a final step. This is the clearest mechanistic difference between this entry and its stimulant siblings, whose dopamine rise needs no opioid receptor.

nodes.description: Delta-9-tetrahydrocannabinol, the main psychotropic constituent of cannabis, is a partial agonist at the CB1 receptor. It is also a partial agonist at CB2, so this entry does not treat the pharmacology as CB1-exclusive; CB1 is the receptor the downstream nodes are about because it is the one whose antagonist blocks the dopamine effect below. Partial agonism matters for the rest of the chain: the response an exogenous partial agonist produces depends on how much receptor is present and on the endocannabinoid tone it competes with, which is the link to the downregulation node.

nodes.description: CB1 activation depresses GABA-A receptor-mediated inhibitory postsynaptic currents in the ventral tegmental area through a presynaptic mechanism, established in rat midbrain slices with a synthetic agonist and blocked by a CB1 antagonist. Removing the GABAergic brake on dopamine neurons is the classical route by which a cannabinoid would raise their firing rate, but that consequence was not measured in the slice preparation and is recorded here as the authors' inference rather than as a result.

nodes.description: Withdrawal shortens abstinence, which is the point at which the cycle closes: the syndrome that follows stopping becomes a reason to resume. The evidence is an association between meeting the withdrawal criteria and a shorter abstinence in a retrospective self-report sample, so the direction is plausible rather than established, and the node is marked provisional. The entry does not claim a measured causal route from withdrawal to resumption.
